hints: Start with what you know for certain - animals are all multicellular and eat other organisms, and plants all photosynthesise. Use those to fill the gaps you can.
Think about yeast and moulds for Fungi - are they all large mushrooms, or can some be single cells? Remember how fungi feed by saprotrophic digestion.
Think about why Plantae is different from Fungi even though both have walls - what pigment and organelle lets plants make their own food?
Think of Protoctista as the varied left-over kingdom - it contains Amoeba, Chlorella and seaweeds, so it can show every combination of the three features.
walkthrough:
Sort Animals, Fungi and Plants By Feeding And Walls**
Animals are all multicellular heterotrophs with no cell walls, so Animalia is no, no, no. Fungi are heterotrophs so no autotrophic nutrition, but yeast are unicellular and all fungi have chitin walls, so Fungi is yes, yes, no. Plants are all multicellular autotrophs with cellulose walls, so Plantae is no, yes, yes.

Remember Protoctista Is The Variable Kingdom**
Protoctista includes unicellular forms like Amoeba and Chlorella and multicellular forms like seaweeds, some with walls and some without, and some photosynthetic and some heterotrophic. That means it can show all three features, so Protoctista is yes, yes, yes.
Final answer: Animalia: no, no, no. Fungi: yes, yes, no. Plantae: no, yes, yes. Protoctista: yes, yes, yes.

hints: Count the cells and the groups of dark-staining chromosomes in each drawing - one cell with one group, one cell with two groups, or two cells with four groups?

Think about what a single line of chromosomes across the middle means compared with chromosomes pulled to opposite ends - lining up is metaphase, moving apart is anaphase, arrived at poles is telophase.
Use the number of cells to separate meiosis I from meiosis II - still in the first division means I, already in two daughter cells dividing again means II.
walkthrough:
Read Chromosome Position In A And B**
In A there is one cell with all the chromosomes lined up in a single dense plate in the centre. That is the metaphase plate. Because homologous chromosomes are still together in one cell it is the first division, so metaphase I. In B there is still one cell but the chromosomes are now in two separate clumps at opposite poles. They have arrived, so this is telophase I.

Use Cell Number To Spot The Second Division In C**
In C a wall has formed to give two cells, and each cell is dividing again with chromosomes separating into two groups inside each cell, giving four groups in total. Division of the two haploid cells is meiosis II, and chromosomes moving apart to poles is anaphase, so anaphase II.
Final answer: A = metaphase I; B = telophase I; C = anaphase II.

hints: Recall the three domains - Eukarya is one, so the other two both contain prokaryotic cells with no nucleus.
Focus on chemistry that looks similar under the microscope but is different at molecular level - what the wall and the membrane are made from.
Think about DNA packaging and protein-making machinery - which domain is more like eukaryotes in its histones and ribosomal RNA sequence?
walkthrough:
Name The Two Prokaryotic Domains**
The three domains are Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Eukarya holds all eukaryotes, so the prokaryotes are Bacteria and Archaea. Both have no membrane-bound nucleus, but their biochemistry is distinct.

Compare Wall, Membrane And Information Molecules**
Bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan while archaeal walls do not. Bacterial membranes use ester-linked unbranched fatty acids while archaeal membranes use ether-linked branched chains. Bacterial DNA has no histones while archaeal DNA is associated with histones like eukaryotes, and their rRNA sequences are different. Any two of these differences plus correct names gives full credit.

Final answer: Bacteria and Archaea. Plus any two: Bacteria walls contain peptidoglycan, Archaea walls lack peptidoglycan; Bacteria membranes have ester-linked unbranched lipids, Archaea have ether-linked branched lipids; Bacteria can form spores, Archaea cannot; Bacteria DNA lacks histones, Archaea DNA has histones; rRNA base sequences / ribosome structure differ.

hints: Viruses have no cells or binary fission, so think about what is inside the protein coat - what type of genetic material can it be?
Once you have the type of nucleic acid, think about its structure - how many strands, and what other structural features like shape or envelope could separate one virus from another?
walkthrough:
Classify By Nucleic Acid Type And Strandedness**
Viruses are acellular so cell features cannot be used. The main basis is their genome: whether it is DNA or RNA, and whether that nucleic acid is single-stranded or double-stranded, linear or circular.

Add Structural Features**
Further separation uses the capsid shape, presence or absence of a lipid envelope, how mRNA is produced, and the host or disease caused. Any two valid points give the two marks.
Final answer: By type of nucleic acid: RNA or DNA; whether single-stranded or double-stranded; e.g. linear or circular, enveloped or non-enveloped, capsid shape, type of disease caused.
